claim: DIP-α is expressed by two identified motor neurons in the Drosophila larval neuromuscular system.
source: Here we show that DIP-α is expressed by two identified motor neurons, while its binding partner Dpr10 is expressed by postsynaptic muscle targets.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dpr10 is expressed by postsynaptic muscle targets.
source: Here we show that DIP-α is expressed by two identified motor neurons, while its binding partner Dpr10 is expressed by postsynaptic muscle targets.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, supported by expression data in Figure 5.

claim: Removal of DIP-α results in loss of specific axonal branches and NMJs formed by MNISN-1s.
source: Removal of either DIP-α or Dpr10 results in loss of specific axonal branches and NMJs formed by one motor neuron, MNISN-1s, while other branches of the MNISN-1s axon develop normally.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is demonstrated by mutant analysis in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Removal of Dpr10 results in loss of specific axonal branches and NMJs formed by MNISN-1s.
source: Removal of either DIP-α or Dpr10 results in loss of specific axonal branches and NMJs formed by one motor neuron, MNISN-1s, while other branches of the MNISN-1s axon develop normally.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is demonstrated by mutant analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Other branches of the MNISN-1s axon develop normally when DIP-α or Dpr10 is removed.
source: Removal of either DIP-α or Dpr10 results in loss of specific axonal branches and NMJs formed by one motor neuron, MNISN-1s, while other branches of the MNISN-1s axon develop normally.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is shown in the connectivity analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The temporal and spatial expression pattern of dpr10 correlates with muscle innervation by MNISN-1s during embryonic development.
source: The temporal and spatial expression pattern of dpr10 correlates with muscle innervation by MNISN-1s during embryonic development.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is demonstrated by developmental expression analysis in Figure 7.

claim: DIP-α and Dpr10 on opposing synaptic partners interact with each other to generate proper motor neuron connectivity.
source: We propose a model whereby DIP-α and Dpr10 on opposing synaptic partners interact with each other to generate proper motor neuron connectivity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila larval neuromuscular system contains 35 identified motor neurons that innervate 30 muscle fibers in each abdominal hemisegment.
source: In each larval abdominal hemisegment, 35 identified motor neurons innervate a set of 30 muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: Each motor neuron chooses one or more specific muscle fibers as synaptic targets in the Drosophila larval neuromuscular system.
source: Each motor neuron chooses one or more specific muscle fibers as synaptic targets, and the map of connections is almost invariant.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: The map of connections between motor neurons and muscle fibers is almost invariant in the Drosophila larval neuromuscular system.
source: Each motor neuron chooses one or more specific muscle fibers as synaptic targets, and the map of connections is almost invariant.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: Drosophila neuromuscular junction synapses are glutamatergic.
source: Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ) synapses are glutamatergic and use orthologs of mammalian AMPA receptors for synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila NMJs.

claim: Drosophila NMJ synapses use orthologs of mammalian AMPA receptors for synaptic transmission.
source: Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ) synapses are glutamatergic and use orthologs of mammalian AMPA receptors for synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila NMJs.

claim: Many scaffolding and regulatory proteins that modulate AMPA receptors are conserved between insects and vertebrates.
source: Many scaffolding and regulatory proteins that modulate these receptors are conserved between insects and vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about conservation of synaptic proteins.

claim: The sizes and strengths of Drosophila NMJs are regulated by retrograde signaling from their postsynaptic muscle targets.
source: The sizes and strengths of Drosophila NMJs are regulated by retrograde signaling from their postsynaptic muscle targets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila NMJ regulation.

claim: Drosophila NMJ synapses exhibit short-term and homeostatic plasticity.
source: In addition to this developmental plasticity, NMJ synapses also exhibit short-term and homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila NMJ properties.

claim: The Drosophila NMJ is a useful genetic model system for excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the mammalian brain.
source: These features make the Drosophila NMJ a useful genetic model system for excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the mammalian brain (Broadie and Bate, 1993; Keshishian et al., 1996; Menon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an established view supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 30 cell-surface proteins have been identified that cause motor axons to mistarget when ubiquitously expressed in muscles.
source: 30 CSPs have been identified that cause motor axons to mistarget when they are ubiquitously expressed in muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citation to Kurusu et al., 2008.

claim: Cell-surface proteins that cause motor axon mistargeting contain a variety of extracellular domain types, including immunoglobulin superfamily domains and leucine-rich repeat sequences.
source: These proteins contain a variety of extracellular domain (XCD) types, including immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) domains and leucine-rich repeat (LRR) sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: Some cell-surface proteins that cause motor axon mistargeting are normally expressed on subsets of muscles in embryos.
source: Some of these proteins are normally expressed on subsets of muscles in embryos, suggesting that they could act as molecular signatures during motor axon targeting (Kurusu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: None of the cell-surface proteins identified thus far are required for innervation of the muscles that express them.
source: However, none of the CSPs identified thus far are required for innervation of the muscles that express them, suggesting that they have partially redundant functions (Chiba et al., 1995; Inaki et al., 2007; Kurusu et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2000; Winberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cell-surface proteins involved in motor axon targeting have partially redundant functions.
source: However, none of the CSPs identified thus far are required for innervation of the muscles that express them, suggesting that they have partially redundant functions (Chiba et al., 1995; Inaki et al., 2007; Kurusu et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2000; Winberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: In loss-of-function mutants lacking cell-surface proteins expressed on muscle fibers or their receptors on motor axons, innervation occurs normally in most cases.
source: In loss-of-function (LOF) mutants lacking CSPs expressed on muscle fibers or the receptors for these proteins on motor axons, innervation occurs normally in most cases.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: There are no published loss-of-function mutations in cell-surface protein genes that cause high-penetrance failures of innervation of specific muscle fibers.
source: To our knowledge, there are no published LOF mutations in CSP genes that cause high-penetrance failures of innervation of specific muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the existing literature.

claim: A network of 21 Dpr proteins and 11 DIP proteins was identified through a global in vitro 'interactome' screen.
source: A network of new candidates for synaptic targeting molecules was recently identified through a global in vitro 'interactome' screen (Özkan et al., 2013). In this network, the 'Dpr-ome', a set of 21 proteins with two IgSF domains, the Dprs, interact in a complex pattern with a set of 11 proteins with three IgSF domains, called DIPs (Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Özkan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Dprs are proteins with two IgSF domains.
source: In this network, the 'Dpr-ome', a set of 21 proteins with two IgSF domains, the Dprs, interact in a complex pattern with a set of 11 proteins with three IgSF domains, called DIPs (Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Özkan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of Dpr proteins.

claim: DIPs are proteins with three IgSF domains.
source: In this network, the 'Dpr-ome', a set of 21 proteins with two IgSF domains, the Dprs, interact in a complex pattern with a set of 11 proteins with three IgSF domains, called DIPs (Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Özkan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of DIP proteins.

claim: Dprs interact in a complex pattern with DIPs.
source: In this network, the 'Dpr-ome', a set of 21 proteins with two IgSF domains, the Dprs, interact in a complex pattern with a set of 11 proteins with three IgSF domains, called DIPs (Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Özkan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Each Dpr and DIP is expressed in a small and unique subset of neurons in the larval ventral nerve cord and pupal brain.
source: We and others have examined the expression patterns of many Dprs and DIPs, and found that each is expressed in a small and unique subset of neurons in the larval ventral nerve cord and pupal brain (Carrillo et al., 2015; Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Loss of dpr11 or DIP-γ produces phenotypes affecting NMJ morphology and retrograde BMP signaling.
source: Loss of either dpr11 or DIP-γ produced phenotypes affecting NMJ morphology and retrograde bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling, but did not alter NMJ connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research by the authors.

claim: Loss of dpr11 or DIP-γ does not alter NMJ connectivity patterns.
source: Loss of either dpr11 or DIP-γ produced phenotypes affecting NMJ morphology and retrograde bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling, but did not alter NMJ connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research by the authors.

claim: DIP-γ is expressed in most motor neurons.
source: DIP-γ is expressed in most motor neurons, so it is unlikely to be involved in recognition of targets by specific motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research by the authors.

claim: DIP-γ is selectively expressed in amacrine neurons that are postsynaptic to photoreceptor neurons that express Dpr11 in the optic lobe.
source: In the optic lobe, however, DIP-γ is selectively expressed in amacrine neurons that are postsynaptic to photoreceptor neurons that express Dpr11, suggesting that Dpr11–DIP-γ interactions may be important in determining synaptic connectivity patterns (Carrillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: For several Dpr–DIP in vitro binding pairs, optic lobe neurons expressing a Dpr are synaptically connected to neurons expressing the cognate DIP.
source: For several other Dpr–DIP in vitro binding pairs, optic lobe neurons expressing a Dpr are also synaptically connected to neurons expressing the cognate DIP (Tan et al., 2015); Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Dprs and DIPs regulate adhesion and sorting of axons of olfactory receptor neurons in the antennal lobe.
source: In the antennal lobe, Dprs and DIPs regulate adhesion and sorting of axons of olfactory receptor neurons (Barish et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: DIP-α is expressed by only two motor neurons in each hemisegment of the larval neuromuscular system.
source: Remarkably, DIP-α is expressed by only two motor neurons in each hemisegment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: There are two types of glutamatergic motor neurons in the larval neuromuscular system: 1b (big boutons) and 1s (small boutons).
source: There are two types of glutamatergic motor neurons in the larval neuromuscular system: 1b (big boutons) and 1s (small boutons).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: Larval muscle fibers are divided into four fields: the ventral, ventrolateral, lateral, and dorsal fields.
source: Larval muscle fibers are divided into four fields: the ventral, ventrolateral, lateral, and dorsal fields.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: Each 1b motor neuron innervates one or two muscle fibers.
source: Each 1b motor neuron innervates one or two muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: The three 1s motor neurons have multiple branches, and each 1s neuron forms branches on most or all of the fibers within a specific muscle field.
source: The three 1s motor neurons have multiple branches, and each 1s neuron forms branches on most or all of the fibers within a specific muscle field (Hoang and Chiba, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s, which synapses on dorsal muscles.
source: DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s, which synapses on dorsal muscles, and in MNISNb/d-1s (also referred to as MNSNb/d-1s), which synapses on ventral and ventrolateral muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: DIP-α is expressed in MNISNb/d-1s, which synapses on ventral and ventrolateral muscles.
source: DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s, which synapses on dorsal muscles, and in MNISNb/d-1s (also referred to as MNSNb/d-1s), which synapses on ventral and ventrolateral muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fate determination and axon guidance of MNISN-1s have been extensively studied in embryos, where it is known as RP2.
source: Fate determination and axon guidance of MNISN-1s have been extensively studied in embryos, where it is known as RP2 (Frasch et al., 1987; Landgraf et al., 1997; Patel et al., 1989; Schmid et al., 1999; Sink and Whitington, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by multiple citations.

claim: MNISN-1s innervates muscles 4, 3, and 2, which are arranged in a ventral→dorsal sequence.
source: A subset of muscles innervated by MNISN-1s axon branches are muscles 4, 3, and 2, which are arranged in a ventral→dorsal sequence (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In DIP-α mutant larvae, the interstitial axon branch onto muscle 4 is always missing.
source: In DIP-α mutant larvae, the interstitial axon branch onto muscle 4 (m4) is always missing, and the branch onto m3 is usually absent.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In DIP-α mutant larvae, the branch onto m3 is usually absent.
source: In DIP-α mutant larvae, the interstitial axon branch onto muscle 4 (m4) is always missing, and the branch onto m3 is usually absent.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The branch onto m2 is always present in DIP-α mutant larvae.
source: The branch onto m2, however, is always present.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: MNISN-1s filopodia are observed in the m4 target area in both wild-type and DIP-α mutant embryos.
source: MNISN-1s filopodia are observed in the m4 target area in both wild-type and DIP-α mutant embryos, but 1s boutons never form on m4 in mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: 1s boutons never form on m4 in DIP-α mutant embryos.
source: MNISN-1s filopodia are observed in the m4 target area in both wild-type and DIP-α mutant embryos, but 1s boutons never form on m4 in mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Nascent axonal projections onto m4 fail to stabilize and convert into NMJs in the absence of DIP-α.
source: This suggests that nascent axonal projections onto m4 fail to stabilize and convert into NMJs in the absence of DIP-α.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from embryonic and larval analysis.

claim: In dpr10 null mutant larvae, the MNISN-1s axon branch onto m4 is missing.
source: We examined phenotypes in the larval neuromuscular system caused by loss of these Dprs, and found that in dpr10 null mutant larvae the MNISN-1s axon branch onto m4 is missing, mimicking the DIP-α mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The dpr10 null mutant phenotype mimics the DIP-α mutant phenotype.
source: We examined phenotypes in the larval neuromuscular system caused by loss of these Dprs, and found that in dpr10 null mutant larvae the MNISN-1s axon branch onto m4 is missing, mimicking the DIP-α mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by comparison of data in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: In third instar larvae, dpr10 is expressed in almost all muscle fibers.
source: In third instar larvae, dpr10 is expressed in almost all muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: During motor axon outgrowth in embryos, dpr10 expression initiates in two muscle fibers in the immediate vicinity of m4.
source: However, during motor axon outgrowth in embryos, dpr10 expression initiates in two muscle fibers in the immediate vicinity of m4, and then comes on in m4 itself around the time at which axon branches appear on this muscle.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: dpr10 expression comes on in m4 around the time at which axon branches appear on this muscle.
source: However, during motor axon outgrowth in embryos, dpr10 expression initiates in two muscle fibers in the immediate vicinity of m4, and then comes on in m4 itself around the time at which axon branches appear on this muscle.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Dpr10 is a muscle recognition cue whose binding to DIP-α on the motor axon triggers recognition and stabilization of the MNISN-1s filopodia on specific muscles.
source: These results suggest that Dpr10 is a muscle recognition cue whose binding to DIP-α on the motor axon triggers recognition and stabilization of the MNISN-1s filopodia on specific muscles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: DIP-α and Dpr10 have expression patterns in adult leg motor neurons and muscles that are qualitatively similar to those seen in the larval neuromuscular system.
source: The accompanying paper (Venkatasubramanian et al., 2019) shows that DIP-α and Dpr10 have expression patterns in adult leg motor neurons and muscles that are qualitatively similar to those seen in the larval neuromuscular system, and that loss of DIP-α or Dpr10 causes failure of DIP-α-expressing leg motor neurons to innervate a subset of their normal muscle targets.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a companion paper, supported by citation.

claim: Loss of DIP-α or Dpr10 causes failure of DIP-α-expressing leg motor neurons to innervate a subset of their normal muscle targets.
source: The accompanying paper (Venkatasubramanian et al., 2019) shows that DIP-α and Dpr10 have expression patterns in adult leg motor neurons and muscles that are qualitatively similar to those seen in the larval neuromuscular system, and that loss of DIP-α or Dpr10 causes failure of DIP-α-expressing leg motor neurons to innervate a subset of their normal muscle targets.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a companion paper, supported by citation.

claim: In both larval and adult leg neuromuscular systems, interactions between DIP-α and Dpr10 control formation of synapses on specific muscle targets.
source: Thus, in both of these neuromuscular systems, interactions between DIP-α and Dpr10 control formation of synapses on specific muscle targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings in the current study and the companion paper.

claim: DIP-α-T2A-GAL4 is a gene trap GAL4 line generated by replacing a splice-trap MiMIC transposable element in the first DIP-α coding intron with a T2A-GAL4 cassette.
source: The GAL4 line was generated by replacing a splice-trap MiMIC transposable element, MI02031 (Venken et al., 2011), in the first DIP-α coding intron with a T2A-GAL4 cassette (Diao and White, 2012), using recombination-mediated cassette exchange (RMCE).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the reporter line.

claim: Most MiMIC-derived GAL4 cassettes faithfully reproduce the expression patterns of the genes into which they are inserted.
source: It has been demonstrated that most MiMIC-derived GAL4 cassettes faithfully reproduce the expression patterns of the genes into which they are inserted (Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: T2A-GAL4 cassettes in coding introns have the feature that GAL4 expression is from a transcript whose translation initiates at the normal ATG of the gene.
source: T2A-GAL4 cassettes in coding introns have the additional feature that GAL4 expression is from a transcript whose translation initiates at the normal ATG of the gene.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of the reporter system.

claim: The expression pattern of GAL4 should correspond to that of the nascent endogenous protein in T2A-GAL4 cassettes.
source: This means that the expression pattern of GAL4 should correspond to that of the nascent endogenous protein.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected behavior of the reporter system.

claim: GAL4-driven reporter expression may not necessarily mimic the expression pattern of an accumulated protein as observed by antibody staining.
source: However, proteins are also subject to post-translational control, so GAL4-driven reporter expression may not necessarily mimic the expression pattern of an accumulated protein as observed by antibody staining (Diao et al., 2015; Venken et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the reporter system, supported by citations.

claim: The first cells to express the DIP-α-T2A-GAL4>UAS-EGFP reporter include a pair of segmentally repeated neurons in the stage 14 embryonic VNC.
source: The first cells to express the DIP-α-T2A-GAL4>UAS-EGFP reporter (DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP) include a pair of segmentally repeated neurons in the stage 14 (st14) embryonic VNC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DIP-α expression persists into late embryonic development.
source: DIP-α expression persists into late embryonic development, and the segmentally repeated pair of dorsal DIP-α+ cells also express the transcription factor Even-skipped (Eve) by st16 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The segmentally repeated pair of dorsal DIP-α+ cells also express the transcription factor Even-skipped (Eve) by st16.
source: DIP-α expression persists into late embryonic development, and the segmentally repeated pair of dorsal DIP-α+ cells also express the transcription factor Even-skipped (Eve) by st16 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The three prominent medially located pairs of Eve+ neurons correspond to the well-characterized aCC, pCC, and RP2 neurons.
source: The three prominent medially located pairs of Eve+ neurons correspond to the well-characterized aCC, pCC, and RP2 neurons (Landgraf et al., 1997; Patel et al., 1989; Schmid et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: pCC is an interneuron.
source: pCC is an interneuron, and aCC is the Ib-type motor neuron that innervates m1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuronal identity.

claim: aCC is the Ib-type motor neuron that innervates m1.
source: pCC is an interneuron, and aCC is the Ib-type motor neuron that innervates m1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuronal identity.

claim: RP2, known as MNISN-1s during larval development, innervates the dorsal muscle field.
source: RP2, known as MNISN-1s during larval development (Figure 1B), innervates the dorsal muscle field.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Based on the stereotyped positions of the neuronal cell bodies in the VNC that express DIP-α, DIP-α is selectively expressed in MNISN-1s/RP2.
source: Based on the stereotyped positions of the neuronal cell bodies in the VNC that express DIP-α, we conclude that DIP-α is selectively expressed in MNISN-1s/RP2 (hereafter referred to as MNISN-1s).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression pattern analysis.

claim: Motor neurons make stereotyped connections with their muscle targets.
source: Motor neurons make stereotyped connections with their muscle targets, allowing us to utilize the innervation pattern of the DIP-α+ Eve+ neuron to identify it.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: Two axons exit the VNC in each hemisegment expressing DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP.
source: Using the same DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP reporter, we observe two axons that exit the VNC in each hemisegment; thus, DIP-α expression persists through embryonic and larval development.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: One of the DIP-α+ axons innervates the dorsal muscles, corresponding to the known connectivity map of MNISN-1s.
source: One of these axons innervates the dorsal muscles (Figure 1C), corresponding to the known connectivity map of MNISN-1s (Hoang and Chiba, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1C and citation.

claim: The other DIP-α+ axon innervates ventral and ventrolateral muscles, corresponding to the connectivity map of MNISNb/d-1s.
source: The other axon innervates ventral and ventrolateral muscles, corresponding to the connectivity map of MNISNb/d-1s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The MNISNb/d-1s cell body is located ventrally within the VNC.
source: The MNISNb/d-1s cell body is located ventrally within the VNC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and is not Eve+.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MNISNb/d-1s is not Eve+.
source: The MNISNb/d-1s cell body is located ventrally within the VNC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and is not Eve+.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Only 1s boutons express the DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP reporter when NMJs on all muscles are visualized with anti-HRP.
source: When NMJs on all muscles are visualized with anti-HRP, it is observed that only 1s boutons express the DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP reporter.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Not all 1s boutons are labeled with the DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP reporter.
source: Not all 1s boutons are labeled with the reporter, however.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: There is a third 1s motor neuron that innervates lateral muscles and does not express DIP-α.
source: There is a third 1s motor neuron that innervates lateral muscles, and this does not express DIP-α.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: DIP-α is expressed by two of the three 1s motor neurons in each abdominal hemisegment.
source: In summary, DIP-α is expressed by two of the three 1s motor neurons in each abdominal hemisegment, and not by any 1b motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the expression findings.

claim: DIP-α is not expressed by any 1b motor neurons.
source: In summary, DIP-α is expressed by two of the three 1s motor neurons in each abdominal hemisegment, and not by any 1b motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the expression findings.

claim: DIP-α is a cell surface protein.
source: DIP-α is a cell surface protein, and analysis of its subcellular localization might provide insights into its function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DIP-α.

claim: DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α is a protein trap constructed by inserting GFP into the reading frame of DIP-α.
source: To address where DIP-α localizes within MNISN-1s, we used a 'protein trap', DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α, constructed by using RMCE to insert GFP into the reading frame of DIP-α, using the same MiMIC as for the T2A-GAL4 replacement (Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015a).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the protein trap.

claim: Protein traps that are expressed well are usually transported to the subcellular compartments where the endogenous protein is located.
source: If such protein traps are expressed well, they usually are transported to the subcellular compartments where the endogenous protein is located.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about protein trap behavior.

claim: During late embryonic development, DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α localized to growth cones prior to muscle innervation.
source: During late embryonic development, DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α localized to growth cones prior to muscle innervation (Figure 1D) and remained distributed to all larval MNISN-1s NMJs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), including m4 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α remained distributed to all larval MNISN-1s NMJs, including m4.
source: During late embryonic development, DIP-α-EGFP-DIP-α localized to growth cones prior to muscle innervation (Figure 1D) and remained distributed to all larval MNISN-1s NMJs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), including m4 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figures 1E and 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Expression patterns support a role for Dpr-DIP interactions in synaptic partner choice.
source: Previously, we and others reported expression patterns that support a role for Dpr-DIP interactions in synaptic partner choice (Carrillo et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The selective expression of DIP-α in two 1s motor neurons suggests that any phenotypes caused by loss of DIP-α might be specific to the axons of these two motor neurons.
source: Given the selective expression of DIP-α in two 1s motor neurons within the neuromuscular system and the localization of DIP-α to presynaptic terminals, we speculated that DIP-α may be involved in targeting of motor axons to muscle fibers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern findings.

claim: The innervation pattern of the larval musculature is almost invariant.
source: The innervation pattern of the larval musculature is almost invariant, so we can readily evaluate changes in connectivity due to alterations in gene function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila neuromuscular system.

claim: MNISN-1s innervates muscles 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20.
source: MNISN-1s innervates most of the dorsal muscles, including muscles 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20 (Hoang and Chiba, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The DIP-α-GAL4 reporter used for expression studies is also an LOF allele.
source: The DIP-α-GAL4 reporter that we used for expression studies is also an LOF allele, since the splice-trap into the GAL4 cassette creates a truncated DIP-α.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the reporter line.

claim: DIP-α is an X-linked gene.
source: Conveniently, due to the fact that DIP-α is an X-linked gene, we could use DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP/+ heterozygous females as controls and DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP/Y hemizygous males as LOF mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the DIP-α gene.

claim: In control DIP-α heterozygous animals, MNISN-1s innervates m4 with a frequency of 77%.
source: In control DIP-α heterozygous animals, MNISN-1s innervates m4 with a frequency of 77%, but we never observed m4-1s branches in DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP hemizygous males (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: m4-1s branches are never observed in DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP hemizygous males.
source: In control DIP-α heterozygous animals, MNISN-1s innervates m4 with a frequency of 77%, but we never observed m4-1s branches in DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP hemizygous males (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2B,D.

claim: The loss of innervation was confirmed with a targeted null deletion mutation in DIP-α (DIP-α1-178) produced by CRISPR.
source: We confirmed the loss of innervation with a targeted null deletion mutation in DIP-α (DIP-α1-178; Figure 2D) produced by CRISPR.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: DIP-α is necessary for innervation of m4 by MNISN-1s.
source: Thus, DIP-α is necessary for innervation of m4 by MNISN-1s.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant analysis.

claim: Examination of MNISNb/d-1s revealed no obvious highly penetrant phenotype upon loss of DIP-α.
source: By contrast, examination of MNISNb/d-1s, the other motor neuron that expresses DIP-α, revealed no obvious highly penetrant phenotype upon loss of DIP-α.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: DIP-α reporters demonstrate that DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s and localizes to MNISN-1s terminals.
source: Although DIP-α reporters demonstrate that DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s and localizes to MNISN-1s terminals, we cannot rule out low-level expression in muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Low-level expression of DIP-α in muscles cannot be ruled out.
source: Although DIP-α reporters demonstrate that DIP-α is expressed in MNISN-1s and localizes to MNISN-1s terminals, we cannot rule out low-level expression in muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the expression analysis.

claim: A C-terminally Myc-tagged UAS-DIP-α construct is able to localize to MNISN-1s NMJs on m4.
source: First, we confirmed that the tagged DIP-α is able to localize to MNISN-1s NMJs on m4 by staining with anti-Myc and anti-DIP-α antibodies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The lack of DIP-α in the MNISN-1s axon in the intersegmental nerve suggests that DIP-α is actively targeted to the NMJ.
source: The lack of DIP-α in the MNISN-1s axon in the intersegmental nerve (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) also suggests that DIP-α is actively targeted to the NMJ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization pattern observed in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Overexpression of DIP-α utilizing eveRN2-GAL4 produced normal m4-1s NMJs.
source: Overexpression of DIP-α utilizing two drivers that are expressed in subsets of motor neurons (eveRN2-GAL4, expressed in MNISN-1s and aCC, plus interneurons; and DIP-α-GAL4, expressed in MNISN-1s and MNISNb/d-1s, plus interneurons) produced normal m4-1s NMJs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Overexpression of DIP-α utilizing DIP-α-GAL4 produced normal m4-1s NMJs.
source: Overexpression of DIP-α utilizing two drivers that are expressed in subsets of motor neurons (eveRN2-GAL4, expressed in MNISN-1s and aCC, plus interneurons; and DIP-α-GAL4, expressed in MNISN-1s and MNISNb/d-1s, plus interneurons) produced normal m4-1s NMJs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Expression of UAS-DIP-α with eveRN2-GAL4 or DIP-α-GAL4 in a DIP-α null background produced complete rescue of the m4-1s phenotype.
source: We expressed these same constructs in a DIP-α null background and found complete rescue of the m4-1s phenotype (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that DIP-α functions in MNISN-1s.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: DIP-α functions in MNISN-1s.
source: We expressed these same constructs in a DIP-α null background and found complete rescue of the m4-1s phenotype (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that DIP-α functions in MNISN-1s.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: RNAi-mediated knock down of DIP-α using Elav-GAL4 or DIP-α-GAL4 produced significant reductions in the frequency of m4-1s innervations.
source: We confirmed that DIP-α is required in MNISN-1s using RNAi-mediated knock down of DIP-α. Utilizing either Elav-GAL4 (pan-neuronal) or DIP-α-GAL4 to drive RNAi expression, we observed significant reductions in the frequency of m4-1s innervations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: Knockdown of DIP-α in muscles using Mef2-GAL4-driven RNAi had no effect on m4-1s.
source: Knockdown of DIP-α in muscles using Mef2-GAL4-driven RNAi had no effect on m4-1s, indicating that DIP-α is required only in the presynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: DIP-α is required only in the presynaptic neuron.
source: Knockdown of DIP-α in muscles using Mef2-GAL4-driven RNAi had no effect on m4-1s, indicating that DIP-α is required only in the presynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Driving pan-neuronal expression of DIP-α with Elav-GAL4 in a wild-type background produced a complete loss of m4-1s.
source: Interestingly, driving pan-neuronal expression of DIP-α with Elav-GAL4 in a wild-type background produced a complete loss of m4-1s, similar to DIP-α LOF.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Expression of DIP-α in muscles using Mef2-GAL4 produced a complete loss of m4-1s.
source: The same result was observed when DIP-α was expressed in muscles using Mef2-GAL4 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Motor neuron axons exit the VNC during embryonic st13-14 and begin to innervate their muscle targets prior to hatching.
source: Motor neuron axons exit the VNC during embryonic st13-14 and begin to innervate their muscle targets prior to hatching (Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: During the larval instars, NMJs formed during embryogenesis expand in order to keep pace with the growth of the muscle fibers.
source: During the larval instars, NMJs formed during embryogenesis expand in order to keep pace with the growth of the muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NMJ development.

claim: MNISN-1s begins to express DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP at st13/14.
source: MNISN-1s begins to express DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP at st13/14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and this expression continues through embryonic st17 and then persists during larval development (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP expression continues through embryonic st17 and then persists during larval development.
source: MNISN-1s begins to express DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP at st13/14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and this expression continues through embryonic st17 and then persists during larval development (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The proper wiring of MNISN-1s requires the coordination of axon guidance, fasciculation, defasciculation, and synaptic partner choice.
source: The proper wiring of MNISN-1s requires the coordination of axon guidance, fasciculation, defasciculation, and synaptic partner choice.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about neuronal wiring.

claim: MNISN-1s innervates the dorsal muscles, the most distal of which is m1.
source: MNISN-1s innervates the dorsal muscles, the most distal of which is m1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MNISN-1s connectivity.

claim: MNISN-1s rarely formed terminal swellings in the proximal muscle field at st15-16, unlike distal muscles.
source: To determine the gross progression of MNISN-1s muscle innervation, we quantified terminal 'swellings' which precede varicosity formation in st15-16 embryos in distal (m1, 2, 9, and 10) and proximal (m3, 4, 19, and 20) muscle fields. MNISN-1s rarely formed terminal swellings in the proximal muscle field at this stage, unlike distal muscles, suggesting that MNISN-1s innervates muscles distal to proximal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MNISN-1s innervates muscles distal to proximal.
source: MNISN-1s rarely formed terminal swellings in the proximal muscle field at this stage, unlike distal muscles, suggesting that MNISN-1s innervates muscles distal to proximal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental analysis.

claim: In control st15 embryos, the MNISN-1s growth cone is easily identifiable in the m1/m2 target area.
source: In control st15 embryos, the MNISN-1s growth cone is easily identifiable in the m1/m2 target area (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: DIP-α nulls are indistinguishable from controls at st15, suggesting that axon guidance is likely not affected.
source: DIP-α nulls are indistinguishable from controls, suggesting that axon guidance is likely not affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: In third instars, proper MNISN-1s innervation of m2 is observed in DIP-α mutants.
source: Additionally, in third instars, we observe proper MNISN-1s innervation of m2 in DIP-α mutants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Defasciculation is typically initiated by filopodia emanating from the growth cone or from the axon shaft.
source: Defasciculation is typically initiated by filopodia emanating from the growth cone (when an entire axon leaves the bundle) or from the axon shaft (when an interstitial branch is being formed).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about axon defasciculation.

claim: In control st17 embryos, there are obvious motor neuron filopodia, including MNISN-1s filopodia that defasciculate from the ISN throughout the dorsal body wall.
source: In control st17 embryos, there are obvious motor neuron filopodia, including MNISN-1s filopodia (identified by their selective expression of DIP-α-GAL4>EGFP) that defasciculate from the ISN throughout the dorsal body wall (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Similar filopodial projections are observed in age-matched DIP-α null embryos, ruling out a function for DIP-α in general defasciculation.
source: We observed similar filopodial projections in age-matched DIP-α null embryos (Figure 3D caret), ruling out a function for DIP-α in general defasciculation (Figure 3C,D asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: During axon pathfinding, filopodia extend and contact both target and non-target muscles.
source: During axon pathfinding, filopodia extend and contact both target and non-target muscles.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about axon pathfinding.

claim: In control embryos, MNISN-1s axon defasciculation and filopodia at m4 are observed beginning in st17.
source: In control embryos, we observe MNISN-1s axon defasciculation and filopodia at m4 beginning in st17 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: MNISN-1s filopodia at more dorsal muscles are evident at earlier stages than st17.
source: MNISN-1s filopodia at more dorsal muscles are evident at earlier stages (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: In DIP-α LOF st17 embryos, MNISN-1s axon protrusions at m4 are still observed.
source: In DIP-α LOF st17 embryos, we still observe MNISN-1s axon protrusions at m4 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the m4-1s branch initially extends but is not properly stabilized due to loss of DIP-α.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: The m4-1s branch initially extends but is not properly stabilized due to loss of DIP-α.
source: In DIP-α LOF st17 embryos, we still observe MNISN-1s axon protrusions at m4 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the m4-1s branch initially extends but is not properly stabilized due to loss of DIP-α.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of filopodia in mutants.

claim: In first instar larvae, 1s boutons are found on m4 in wild-type.
source: In first instar larvae, 1s boutons are found on m4 in wild-type (Figure 3E), but we never observed a 1s bouton on m4 in DIP-α mutants (Figure 3F; 64 hemisegments examined).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: A 1s bouton on m4 is never observed in DIP-α mutants in first instar larvae.
source: In first instar larvae, 1s boutons are found on m4 in wild-type (Figure 3E), but we never observed a 1s bouton on m4 in DIP-α mutants (Figure 3F; 64 hemisegments examined).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: MNISN-1s filopodia still contact m4 in the absence of DIP-α, but fail to establish a stable interstitial branch.
source: These data suggest that MNISN-1s filopodia still contact m4 in the absence of DIP-α, but fail to establish a stable interstitial branch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental analysis.

claim: Previous studies reported that MNISN-1s innervates eight dorsal muscles (1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20).
source: Previous studies reported that MNISN-1s innervates eight dorsal muscles (1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20) (Hoang and Chiba, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: A detailed analysis of innervation shows that MNISN-1s targets m2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20 almost invariantly.
source: A detailed analysis of innervation shows that MNISN-1s targets m2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 19, and 20 almost invariantly (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4A,C.

claim: m1, the most dorsal muscle, is usually not innervated by MNISN-1s in control animals.
source: However, m1, the most dorsal muscle, is usually not innervated in control animals.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: In a DIP-α null background, m1 consistently has 1s branches.
source: We repeated this analysis in a DIP-α null background and observed interesting alterations in connectivity. First, m1, which rarely has 1s innervation, consistently had 1s branches (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Two muscles, m11 and m18, which are never innervated by MNISN-1s in controls, sometimes receive ectopic 1s branches upon removal of DIP-α.
source: Second, two muscles, m11 and m18, which are never innervated by MNISN-1s in controls, now sometimes receive ectopic 1s branches upon removal of DIP-α.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Muscles adjacent to m4 also lose 1s innervation in DIP-α mutants.
source: Third, muscles adjacent to m4 also lose 1s innervation in mutants (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: m3, 19, and 20 show major reductions in 1s branch frequency in DIP-α mutants.
source: Specifically, m3, 19, and 20 show major reductions in 1s branch frequency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The more dorsal muscles in the dorsal muscle field gain 1s branches (m1, 2, 11, 18) in DIP-α mutants, while more ventral muscles (m3, 4, 19, 20) lose innervation.
source: It is interesting to note that the more dorsal muscles in the dorsal muscle field gain 1s branches (m1, 2, 11, 18), while more ventral muscles (m3, 4, 19, 20) lose innervation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the connectivity analysis.

claim: m2 has an approximately 2-fold increase in the number of MNISN-1s branches in DIP-α mutants.
source: m2, for example, has an approximately 2-fold increase in the number of MNISN-1s branches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dpr6 is expressed in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC, including MNISN-1s and aCC.
source: dpr6-T2A-GAL4>EGFP shows dpr6 expression in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC, including MNISN-1s and aCC (Figure 5A), and analysis of the larval bodywall reveals that dpr6 is expressed in type 1b and 1s motor neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: dpr6 is expressed in type 1b and 1s motor neurons in the larval bodywall.
source: dpr6-T2A-GAL4>EGFP shows dpr6 expression in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC, including MNISN-1s and aCC (Figure 5A), and analysis of the larval bodywall reveals that dpr6 is expressed in type 1b and 1s motor neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: dpr6 and DIP-α are co-expressed in MNISN-1s.
source: Thus, dpr6 and DIP-α are co-expressed in MNISN-1s.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression analysis.

claim: dpr10 is expressed in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC.
source: We next investigated dpr10 expression using a dpr10-T2A-GAL4 reporter. dpr10 is found in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) but, unlike dpr6 and DIP-α, it is not expressed in embryonic MNISN-1s (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dpr10 is not expressed in embryonic MNISN-1s.
source: We next investigated dpr10 expression using a dpr10-T2A-GAL4 reporter. dpr10 is found in subsets of cells in the embryonic VNC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) but, unlike dpr6 and DIP-α, it is not expressed in embryonic MNISN-1s (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: dpr10 is prominently expressed in third instar larval muscles, including m4.
source: dpr10 is prominently expressed in third instar larval muscles, including m4 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Some dpr10 signal is detected in the nerves, suggesting that dpr10 is expressed in neurons that have axons in the periphery.
source: Some signal is detected in the nerves (Figure 5D caret), suggesting that dpr10 is expressed in neurons that have axons in the periphery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern observed in Figure 5D.

claim: V5 staining of UAS-Dpr10-V5 expressed in muscles is selectively found at NMJs, surrounding both 1b and 1s boutons.
source: To define Dpr10 localization, we expressed a UAS-Dpr10-V5 construct in muscles. Remarkably, V5 staining was selectively found at NMJs, surrounding both 1b and 1s boutons, indicating that the protein localizes to the postsynaptic side of NMJs (Figure 5E; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1B for anti-V5 staining of control NMJs).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: Dpr10 localizes to the postsynaptic side of NMJs.
source: To define Dpr10 localization, we expressed a UAS-Dpr10-V5 construct in muscles. Remarkably, V5 staining was selectively found at NMJs, surrounding both 1b and 1s boutons, indicating that the protein localizes to the postsynaptic side of NMJs (Figure 5E; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1B for anti-V5 staining of control NMJs).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization experiment.

claim: DIP-α-AP5 shows minimal binding to wild type tissue.
source: We used a recombinant DIP-α fused with pentameric alkaline phosphatase (DIP-α-AP5) to probe dissected, unfixed third instar larvae. After subsequent fixation, DIP-α-AP5 was then detected by immunofluorescence, using antibodies against the AP epitope. In wild type animals, DIP-α-AP5 shows minimal binding to tissue (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5F.

claim: Upon ectopic postsynaptic expression of Dpr10-V5 in muscles, strong labeling of the postsynaptic membrane surrounding boutons is observed with DIP-α-AP5.
source: However, upon ectopic postsynaptic expression of Dpr10-V5 in muscles, we observed strong labeling of the postsynaptic membrane surrounding boutons (Figure 5G), suggesting that DIP-α is able to directly bind to Dpr10.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: DIP-α is able to directly bind to Dpr10 in tissue.
source: However, upon ectopic postsynaptic expression of Dpr10-V5 in muscles, we observed strong labeling of the postsynaptic membrane surrounding boutons (Figure 5G), suggesting that DIP-α is able to directly bind to Dpr10.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding assay results.

claim: Endogenous muscle Dpr10 interacts transsynaptically with DIP-α in MNISN-1s terminals.
source: This observation supports a model whereby endogenous muscle Dpr10 interacts transsynaptically with DIP-α in MNISN-1s terminals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the binding assay results.

claim: Dpr10 interacts with DIP-α both in vitro and in tissue.
source: Since Dpr10 interacts with DIP-α, both in vitro and in tissue, and is able to localize to the postsynaptic membrane, we decided to investigate the requirement of dpr10 for MNISN-1s innervation of m4.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous findings.

claim: 1s boutons have less extensive SSR relative to 1b boutons.
source: In order to distinguish 1s and 1b terminals, we stained for a subsynaptic reticulum (SSR) marker, Discs-Large (Dlg), and identified 1s boutons by their less extensive SSR relative to 1b boutons (Guan et al., 1996) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In dpr1014-5 mutants, loss of almost 100% of 1s boutons on m4 is observed.
source: We examined a CRISPR-generated null deletion mutant of dpr10, dpr1014-5. In this mutant, we observed loss of almost 100% of 1s boutons on m4 (Figure 6B and D), similar to the DIP-α null phenotype (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Dorsal MNISN-1s innervation (m1, 2, 9, and 10) is largely unaltered in dpr10 mutants.
source: Dorsal MNISN-1s innervation (m1, 2, 9, and 10) was largely unaltered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 1b boutons are still present on m4 in dpr10 mutants.
source: 1b boutons were still present on m4 (Figure 6B), indicating that Dpr10 is specifically required for MNISN-1s innervation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Dpr10 is specifically required for MNISN-1s innervation.
source: 1b boutons were still present on m4 (Figure 6B), indicating that Dpr10 is specifically required for MNISN-1s innervation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant analysis.

claim: dpr6-T2A-GAL4/Df mutants have no m4-1s phenotype.
source: Also, dpr6-T2A-GAL4/Df mutants have no m4-1s phenotype, and do not produce any other detectable alterations in MNISN-1s (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The role of DIP-α in formation of the m4-1s branch is likely to be mediated through its interactions with Dpr10.
source: Thus, the role of DIP-α in formation of the m4-1s branch is likely to be mediated through its interactions with Dpr10.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant analysis of dpr6 and dpr10.

claim: Presynaptic expression of dpr10-RNAi with DIP-α-GAL4 did not affect MNISN-1s targeting to m4.
source: Presynaptic expression of dpr10-RNAi with DIP-α-GAL4 did not affect MNISN-1s targeting to m4 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: Driving dpr10-RNAi in muscles (Mef2-GAL4) phenocopied the dpr10 null mutation, producing an almost complete loss of m4-1s branches.
source: However, driving dpr10-RNAi in muscles (Mef2-GAL4) phenocopied the dpr10 null mutation, producing an almost complete loss of m4-1s branches (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: dpr10 is required in muscles.
source: This result indicates that dpr10 is required in muscles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of dpr10-RNAi produced a partial loss of m4-1s.
source: Interestingly, pan-neuronal expression of dpr10-RNAi produced a partial loss of m4-1s (Figure 6F), suggesting that Dpr10 expression in a non-1s neuron also contributes to proper targeting.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: Dpr10 expression in a non-1s neuron contributes to proper targeting.
source: Interestingly, pan-neuronal expression of dpr10-RNAi produced a partial loss of m4-1s (Figure 6F), suggesting that Dpr10 expression in a non-1s neuron also contributes to proper targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi experiment results.

claim: Dpr10-V5 localizes to NMJs when it is expressed in muscles.
source: We also attempted to rescue the m4-1s phenotype using the UAS-Dpr10-V5 construct described above. Dpr10-V5 localizes to NMJs when it is expressed in muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Expression of Dpr10-V5 from pan-neuronal (Elav-GAL4) or muscle (Mef2-GAL4) drivers reduced the frequency of m4-1s branches, even in a wild-type background.
source: However, we observed that expression of Dpr10-V5 from pan-neuronal (Elav-GAL4) or muscle (Mef2-GAL4) drivers reduced the frequency of m4-1s branches, even in a wild-type background (Figure 6E), similar to DIP-α GOF.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of Dpr10 almost eliminated m4-1s branches.
source: Pan-neuronal expression of Dpr10 almost eliminated m4-1s branches.
